target.title: fix(whatsapp): Add group admin privacy controls
target.body:
Closes #69233

## What changed

This adds an optional per-group WhatsApp admin override via `channels.whatsapp.groups.<jid>.admin` and wildcard `channels.whatsapp.groups."*".admin`.

When an admin is configured for a group scope:
- the configured E.164 number bypasses mention gating for that group
- non-admin group members cannot run slash commands in that group
- the configured admin remains able to run slash commands for that group

When no admin is configured, the existing group command authorization behavior is preserved.

## Why

The issue described a privacy gap in mixed-trust WhatsApp groups: non-admin members could still probe bot behavior through mentions and slash commands. The first pass of this feature covered the basic config and enforcement, but upstream readiness also needed the behavior pinned down for wildcard group config and for the no-admin-configured fallback path.

## User impact

Users can now designate a WhatsApp group admin by phone number and use that as a privacy boundary for command discovery in group chats.

This is intentionally backwards-compatible:
- groups without `admin` continue using the existing command authorization rules
- exact-group and wildcard group config both work
- docs now describe the new config key

## Root cause

OpenClaw already had group policy, allowlists, and mention gating, but it did not have a per-group owner/admin concept for WhatsApp. That meant there was no narrow way to let a trusted operator manage the bot in a group without exposing command access to other participants covered by broader allowlist rules.

## Validation

- `npm exec pnpm@10.9.0 -- test extensions/whatsapp/src/group-policy.test.ts`
- `npm exec pnpm@10.9.0 -- test extensions/whatsapp/src/inbound/access-control.test.ts`

target.title: add option for MCP apps support
target.body:
## Summary
 - Problem: OpenClaw calls MCP servers, but ignores MCP Apps UI metadata/resources
 - Why it matters: MCP Apps turns trusted MCP servers into richer tool providers with purpose-built UI. Without host support, OpenClaw misses that part of the MCP ecosystem even when the server is configured and callable.
- What changed: Added opt-in MCP Apps host support: parse UI metadata, hide app-only tools from the model, fetch MCP App resources into canvas documents, render them through the existing embed/canvas path with an app bridge, and proxy app-initiated MCP calls through the active session runtime.
- What changed: Added restart/reload hardening for restored app views, wider assistant canvas layout, docs, config schema support,tests, and a security-audit warning when `mcp.apps.enabled=true`.
-  What did NOT change (scope boundary): Normal MCP tool execution still works without MCP Apps. MCP Apps are default-off behind `mcp.apps.enabled`; this does not add a marketplace, new MCP server examples, or plugin-only architecture.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [x] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [x] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)
- MCP app-only tools are not materialized for the model.
- MCP Apps UI payloads are only fetched/rendered when `mcp.apps.enabled=true`.
- App bridge calls are rejected when MCP Apps are disabled.
- App bridge calls enforce app-callable tool visibility.
- Persisted/restored app views can recreate an MCP runtime after gateway restart.
- Existing `[embed]` canvas rendering remains the fallback path when MCP Apps metadata is absent or disabled.

- Target test or file:
  - New opt-in config: `mcp.apps.enabled`.
  - Default behavior is unchanged for normal MCP tools; MCP Apps UI rendering is disabled by default.
  - When enabled, trusted MCP servers can render interactive app views in chat using the existing canvas/embed path.
  - MCP Apps views may call app-visible MCP tools through the active session runtime.
  - App-only MCP tools are hidden from the model.
  - `openclaw security audit` now warns when MCP Apps are enabled.
  - Docs now describe MCP Apps setup, scope, and security considerations. 
- Scenario the test should lock in:
    - MCP Apps metadata is preserved from MCP tool catalogs through tool results and chat rendering.
    - App-only tools are hidden from the model.
    - Model-only tools are blocked from app bridge calls.
    - MCP Apps UI rendering and bridge proxy calls require `mcp.apps.enabled=true`.
    - Restored app views can recreate an MCP runtime after gateway restart.
    - Existing canvas/embed rendering remains the fallback when MCP Apps are disabled or metadata is absent.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:
    - The feature crosses runtime materialization, gateway proxying, config/bootstrap, and UI rendering. Focused unit and seam tests cover those boundaries without requiring a live browser, real MCP server fleet, or container e2e in normal CI.
- Existing test that already covers this (if any):
    - Existing canvas/embed tests covered generic iframe rendering, but not MCP Apps metadata, app-only visibility, app bridge calls, or restored MCP runtime behavior.

  ## User-visible / Behavior Changes
  - New opt-in config: `mcp.apps.enabled`.
  - Default behavior is unchanged for normal MCP tools; MCP Apps UI rendering is disabled by default.
  - When enabled, trusted MCP servers can render interactive app views in chat using the existing canvas/embed path.
  - MCP Apps views may call app-visible MCP tools through the active session runtime.
  - App-only MCP tools are hidden from the model.
  - `openclaw security audit` now warns when MCP Apps are enabled.
  - Docs now describe MCP Apps setup, scope, and security considerations.
  
## Diagram (if applicable)

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
    A[MCP server tool] --> B[Tool result with UI metadata]
    B --> C[OpenClaw MCP runtime]
    C --> D[Fetch MCP App HTML resource]
    D --> E[Canvas document / existing embed path]
    E --> F[Control UI mcp-app-view iframe]
    F --> G[AppBridge]
    G --> H[Gateway mcp.* proxy]
    H --> C
  ```
## Security Impact (required)
  - New permissions/capabilities? (`Yes/No`): Yes
  - Secrets/tokens handling changed? (`Yes/No`): No
  - New/changed network calls? (`Yes/No`): No for normal MCP transport; Yes in the sense that enabled MCP Apps can make app-initiated MCP calls back through the existing MCP session runtime.
  - Command/tool execution surface changed? (`Yes/No`): Yes
  - Data access scope changed? (`Yes/No`): Yes
  - If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation:
    - Risks:
       - MCP servers with MCP Apps support can provide HTML/JS UI resources that OpenClaw renders in chat.
       -  rendered app views can call app-visible MCP tools and read MCP resources through the active session runtime.
       - app views receive the tool input/result payload they are rendering.
    - Mitigations:
        - MCP Apps are default-off behind `mcp.apps.enabled=true`.
        - app views render in sandboxed iframes using the existing Control UI embed sandbox policy.
        - app-only tools are hidden from the model, and model-only tools are blocked from app bridge calls.
        - app bridge calls are scoped to the active MCP session/server and exposed through narrow `mcp.*` gateway methods.
        - `openclaw security audit` warns when MCP Apps are enabled.
- Trust model: enabling MCP Apps means trusting the configured MCP servers not only as tool providers, but also as UI code providers.

  ## Repro + Verification

  ### Environment
  - OS: macOS
  - Runtime/container: local OpenClaw container via Podman
  - Model/provider: Claude Sonnet 4.6
  - Integration/channel (if any): Control UI chat with configured MCP servers
  - Relevant config (redacted):

```json
  {
    "mcp": {
      "apps": {
        "enabled": true
      },
      "servers": {
        "system-monitor": {
          "command": "npx",
          "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-system-monitor", "--stdio"]
        },
        "pdf": {
          "command": "npx",
          "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-pdf", "--stdio"]
        },
        "qr": {
          "url": "http://127.0.0.1:3108/mcp",
          "transport": "streamable-http"
        }
      }
    }
  }
```

### Steps
  1. Build and run an OpenClaw image from this branch.
  2. Enable MCP Apps with openclaw config set mcp.apps.enabled true --strict-json.
  3. Configure the system-monitor, pdf, and qr MCP servers.
  4. Start the QR MCP sidecar if using the QR example.
  5. Start a fresh chat/session in the Control UI.
  6. Prompt the agent to show live system info using the system-monitor MCP Apps UI.
  7. Prompt the agent to generate a QR code using the QR MCP Apps UI.
  8. Prompt the agent to display https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762 using the PDF MCP Apps UI.
  9. Restart the OpenClaw container and reload the Control UI.
  10. Confirm the persisted PDF app view reloads and reconnects.

### Expected

  - Normal MCP tools still work.
  - With mcp.apps.enabled=true, MCP Apps UI resources render as interactive embedded app views.
  - System monitor renders a live monitor UI.
  - QR renders an embedded QR UI.
  - PDF renders an interactive PDF viewer.
  - Restored app views can reconnect after gateway/container restart.
  - With mcp.apps.enabled=false, app bridge calls are rejected and MCP Apps render through the normal fallback path instead of the app bridge.

### Actual

  - Verified locally with system-monitor, QR, and PDF MCP Apps examples.
  - Verified upstream image comparison: upstream can call the MCP servers but does not render the MCP Apps UI resources.
  - Verified restart/reload behavior for the PDF app view.

Attach at least one:

- [ ] Failing test/log before + passing after
- [ ] Trace/log snippets
- [x] Screenshot/recording
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

## Human Verification (required)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aaa93975-4406-493e-a060-4ac64763704b

## Review Conversations

- [ ] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR.
- [ ] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment.

If a bot review conversation is addressed by this PR, resolve that conversation yourself. Do not leave bot review conversation cleanup for maintainers.

## Compatibility / Migration

- Backward compatible? (`Yes/No`) Yes
- Config/env changes? (`Yes/No`) Yes
- Migration needed? (`Yes/No`) No
- If yes, exact upgrade steps:
    - No migration is required for existing installs. MCP Apps support is default-off.
    - To enable it, set:
      ```bash
      openclaw config set mcp.apps.enabled true --strict-json
      ```
    - Configure MCP servers that expose MCP Apps / `mcp-ui` resources.
    - Restart OpenClaw so the updated config is loaded.

## Risks and Mitigations

  - Risk: Enabling MCP Apps allows configured MCP servers to provide HTML/JS UI that renders inside OpenClaw.
    - Mitigation: Feature is opt-in via `mcp.apps.enabled`; app UI renders in a sandboxed iframe; docs and security audit call out the trust boundary.
  - Risk: App views can call app-visible MCP tools/resources through the bridge, increasing the practical surface area of a trusted MCP server.
    - Mitigation: Bridge is scoped to MCP app methods only; model-only tools are blocked from app bridge calls; app-only tools are hidden from the model.
  - Risk: Restored chat views may need to reconnect to MCP runtimes after a container restart.
    - Mitigation: Gateway proxy lazily recreates the session MCP runtime from config when an app bridge call arrives and no runtime is currently active.
  - Risk: Servers without MCP Apps support, or installs with the feature disabled, should not regress.
    - Mitigation: Existing MCP tool execution path remains unchanged; UI falls back to the existing embed/canvas rendering behavior when MCP Apps are disabled or metadata is absent.

target.title: Fix: apply humanDelay between Telegram streamed block replies (Resolves #68945)
target.body:
Fixes #68945.

The Telegram block-streaming path does not wire `resolveHumanDelayConfig(cfg, agentId)` into `dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher`, so `agents.defaults.humanDelay` / per-agent `humanDelay` overrides have no effect on Telegram block replies.

This change matches the pattern already in Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, Matrix, MS Teams, Feishu, Tlon, and Mattermost: import `resolveHumanDelayConfig` through the existing `bot-message-dispatch.agent.runtime.ts` seam and pass its result as `dispatcherOptions.humanDelay` in `bot-message-dispatch.ts`.

target.title: fix(gateway): prefer current route delivery context
target.body:
## Summary

- Fixes gateway agent delivery resolution so a concrete current request route (`channel`, `to`, `accountId`, `threadId`) wins over stale persisted session `deliveryContext` fields when the channels conflict.
- Clears stale route fields on channel switches when the new request does not provide replacement `to`/`accountId`/`threadId` values, avoiding mixed-channel routes.
- Preserves existing session-route behavior for normal follow-ups, `channel=last`, and same-channel existing-session routes.
- Compares same-channel targets through the channel parser so equivalent encodings do not clear stored threads.
- Populates `runContext.currentChannelId` from the resolved delivery target so downstream message-tool fallback inference sees the active route.
- Adds regression tests for the #68378 shape, channel-only stale-route clearing, same-channel partial updates, and canonical equivalent targets.

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #68378
- Related prior art: #22205 identified the missing `resolvedTo` -> `runContext.currentChannelId` propagation, but that PR is closed unmerged and does not address stale delivery-context precedence.
- Related but not duplicates: #45514, #65847, #33619, #39557, #51812, #52204 all describe adjacent multi-channel/stale-routing problems or other delivery paths; none is an open satisfactory PR for this gateway agent route-precedence bug.

## Root Cause / Diagnosis

`src/gateway/server-methods/agent.ts` built `requestDeliveryHint` from the active gateway request, but then merged it with the stored session `deliveryContext` in a way that made persisted fields authoritative. That let stale persisted fields, such as Feishu `channel`/`to`, override a current Discord request before the agent command and session update were assembled. The same path also did not pass the resolved target into `runContext.currentChannelId`, so tool fallback routing could miss the current route even when `resolvedTo` was known.

A second edge case appears when the request changes only `channel`: route-field fallback must not pair a new channel with stale `lastTo`/`lastAccountId`/`lastThreadId` from the old channel.

A third edge case appears when the request and session refer to the same target with different channel-owned encodings, such as Slack `C1` and `channel:C1`: raw string comparison can falsely treat that as a target change and clear the stored thread.

## Fix

- Detect when a concrete request channel conflicts with the stored session delivery channel.
- In that cross-channel conflict case, let the current request delivery hint win and use persisted delivery metadata only as fallback for fields provided by the current route.
- Clear stale last-route fields when the current channel conflicts and no replacement field is available.
- For same-channel route conflicts, preserve unchanged target/account/thread fields unless the concrete target itself changes.
- Compare request/session targets using the channel parser before treating `to` as a target change, preserving stored threads for equivalent target spellings.
- For non-conflict cases, keep existing session delivery precedence so `channel=last`, normal follow-ups, and existing subagent routes behave as before.
- Pass `resolvedTo` into `runContext.currentChannelId` alongside the existing channel/account/thread context.
- Lock the behavior with regression tests that start from stale Feishu metadata, assert Discord wins or stale route fields are cleared, preserve partial same-channel updates, and keep Slack threads when `C1` and `channel:C1` are equivalent.

## Duplicate Sweep

Searched GitHub issues/PRs for combinations of `#68378`, Discord/Feishu wrong-channel delivery, stale `deliveryContext`, gateway agent delivery, `currentChannelId`, and multi-channel session routing. Closest results:

- #22205: overlapping `currentChannelId` propagation only; closed unmerged; no stale context precedence fix or regression for #68378.
- #35451: broader `chat.send`/cron canonical route derivation; closed unmerged; different call sites.
- #67508: target-agent bound account propagation for Matrix subagent spawns; adjacent account routing, different bug.
- #45514, #65847, #33619, #39557, #51812, #52204: related issue reports/bug class, not acceptable duplicate PRs for this exact gateway agent request-route overwrite.

Conclusion: no duplicate or already-satisfactory PR found for #68378.

## Attribution

- Thanks @Suidge for the #68378 report and follow-up logs that isolated Discord input being delivered through Feishu outbound.
- Thanks @Galygious for prior analysis in #22205 around forwarding `resolvedTo` into `runContext.currentChannelId`; this PR incorporates that same missing-context piece and adds the route-precedence fix needed for #68378.

## Testing

Fresh `origin/main` base: `64089fd15ed4ba8296612b1a622d11b5662c8b96`

- `pnpm test -- src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts -t "uses the current request route"`
- `pnpm test -- src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts`
- `pnpm test -- src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts -t "preserves the stored thread when the request target is canonically equivalent"`
- `pnpm test -- src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts src/gateway/server.agent.gateway-server-agent-a.test.ts src/gateway/server.agent.gateway-server-agent-b.test.ts src/gateway/server.agent.subagent-delivery-context.test.ts`

The final command covers the CI shard failures observed after the first draft and now passes locally with 71 tests.

Scoped lint note: `pnpm lint -- src/gateway/server-methods/agent.ts src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts` is currently blocked before linting these files by the existing `src/agents/skills/*` plugin SDK boundary type errors already present on `origin/main`.

## Review Follow-up

- Addressed and resolved Codex review thread about clearing stale route fields on channel-switch merges in `5825aede6c7568f8cec2af2653d4851bf3296d78`.
- Addressed and resolved Codex review thread about preserving unchanged same-channel route fields in `d8f4d09a343f30d82df2bdeea9541a707923a72d`.
- Addressed and resolved Codex review thread about canonical target comparison in `af7506771a0fd734024ecc2b51b23b7945f27b21`.

## Security Impact

- New permissions/capabilities? No
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- New/changed network calls? No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- Data access scope changed? No

The change narrows routing behavior to prefer the active request route only when it conflicts with stale persisted delivery metadata, and preserves stored thread context for equivalent same-channel target spellings.

target.body:
Fixes #98865

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw backup create` could still traverse disposable agent runtime caches, browser cache/resource-cache trees, retired archive copies, and state-side transient sidecars. Those paths can bloat archives or race with tar even though they have no restoration value.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing backup archive path already centralizes volatile filtering through `isVolatileBackupPath`, so this extends that owner boundary instead of adding another archive-time special case. Browser filtering is intentionally scoped to cache-like directories under managed `user-data` paths so durable profile files such as `Preferences` and `Login Data` remain eligible for backup. `.lock` and `.partial` files are scoped to cache, queue, and tmp scratch roots so installed plugin source under `state/extensions` stays backed up; SQLite sidecars stay under the backup SQLite snapshot consistency guard instead of being treated as generic volatile files.

Issue #98865 was closed manually rather than by a merged runtime fix. I checked current `upstream/main` at `4e6933c84f`, the issue closure events, and related PR search; I found a docs-only open PR (#99007) but no equivalent runtime fix on main.

## User Impact

Backups now skip more disposable runtime/cache files and retired archive copies, reducing archive size and avoiding avoidable live-file races while preserving durable OpenClaw state, browser profile data, installed plugin source files, and SQLite consistency checks.

target.title: fix: normalize visible assistant output before delivery
target.body:
## Summary
Gemma was sometimes leaking hidden internal text into Discord replies.
This PR makes OpenClaw clean the final reply in one shared place before sending it.
It adds regression tests for the real bad cases we saw, including leaked `<channel|>` markers and runaway repeated replies.
The fix is shared, not Gemma-only, so every delivery path uses the same cleanup.


## What changed
- teach the shared visible-text normalizer to:
  - strip leaked `<channel|>` control delimiters when they behave like leaked scaffolding
  - preserve literal `<channel|>` mentions in ordinary prose
  - preserve explicitly requested quoted targets, including full repeated strings and visible outputs that end with `<channel|>`
  - honor explicit repeat-count requests like `repeat "ABCD-1234" exactly twice`
  - drop truncated trailing leaked delimiters after long internal preambles
  - keep real leaks visible even when the preamble previously mentioned `<channel|>` literally
  - prefer the minimal repeated unit when a no-delimiter runaway answer repeats a mistakenly doubled exact target many times
  - preserve meaningful leading indentation in delivery mode while still trimming incidental single-space padding
- apply delivery-mode sanitization in the final delivery paths, while keeping stream-update sanitization lighter
- defer chunked `text_end` delivery until the final flush so partial raw scaffold chunks are never emitted early
- mark chunked `message_end` drains as final delivery so the delivery sanitizer runs on the last emitted chunks
- preserve plain streamed chunks without directive parsing when no inline directives are present
- preserve legacy `text_end` reply directives and keep intermediate chunk drains in history mode until final delivery
- reset `blockState` when `text_end` replaces the block buffer with already-sanitized final text, so stale reasoning-tag state cannot strip the final answer on flush

## Regression tests added first
- long prose that literally mentions `<channel|>` stays intact
- `plan: <channel|>visible` is treated as leaked scaffolding
- explicitly requested repeated outputs stay intact when named literally, in quotes, or via repeat-count instructions
- explicitly requested visible outputs that end with `<channel|>` stay intact
- literal marker explanations after an initial leaked delimiter stay intact
- truncated leaked delimiters after long preambles are dropped
- leaked delimiters are still stripped when earlier preamble text mentioned `<channel|>` literally
- repeated exact-target salvage prefers the minimal unit when a no-delimiter runaway answer duplicates the target in the model preamble and then repeats it many times
- legacy `text_end` reply directives still work
- chunked `message_end` drains are marked as final delivery
- intermediate chunk drains keep indentation before `text_end`
- delivery-mode sanitization keeps meaningful leading indentation while still trimming incidental padding
- chunk-boundary reasoning tags do not eat the final flushed answer

## Verification
- failing regressions were added first and reproduced locally before the fixes
- focused tests:
  - `pnpm exec vitest run src/shared/text/repeated-visible-suffix.test.ts src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`
  - `pnpm exec vitest run src/shared/text/repeated-visible-suffix.test.ts src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts src/agents/pi-embedded-utils.strip-model-special-tokens.test.ts src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.handlers.messages.test.ts src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.reply-tags.test.ts src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.subscribe-embedded-pi-session.emits-block-replies-text-end-does-not.test.ts src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.subscribe-embedded-pi-session.keeps-indented-fenced-blocks-intact.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/reply-utils.test.ts`
- `pnpm build`
- live Discord probe on `vllm/gemma4-e4b` after restarting the local gateway on this branch:
  - Looper prompt: `reply with exactly pr68986-live2-1776657698 and nothing else`
  - Bob visible Discord reply: `pr68986-live2-1776657698`

target.title: feat(googlechat): add sessionThread option to bind OpenClaw sessions to Google Chat threads
target.body: AI-assisted: yes (Claude Opus 4.7). ## Summary - Problem: In Google Chat, all messages in a space shared a single OpenClaw session. Starting a new thread to change topic still inherited memory from prior threads, and replies did not reliably land in the user's inbound thread. - Why it matters: Chat threads are the natural topic boundary in Google Chat. Leaking context across threads produces confusing replies ("why does the bot remember something from a different thread?"), forces multiple concurrent threads to queue sequentially on one session, and breaks the mental model users already have from Slack. Requested in #13373. - What changed: Added an opt-in `sessionThread` channel option. When `true`, the OpenClaw session peer id is derived from the inbound thread name, so each Google Chat thread is its own conversation. Replies are now threaded via `thread.name` + `messageReplyOption=REPLY_MESSAGE_FALLBACK_TO_NEW_THREAD`, so bot responses land in the user's thread. - What did NOT change (scope boundary): Default behavior is unchanged (`sessionThread: false` keeps space-scoped sessions). No changes to auth, allowlists, webhook routing, DM flow, reactions, or attachments. No slash commands / `/focus`-style bindings added (see "future work" below). ## Change Type (select all) - [x] Bug fix - [x] Feature - [ ] Refactor required for the fix - [x] Docs - [ ] Security hardening - [ ] Chore/infra ## Scope (select all touched areas) - [ ] Gateway / orchestration - [ ] Skills / tool execution - [ ] Auth / tokens - [ ] Memory / storage - [x] Integrations - [ ] API / contracts - [ ] UI / DX - [ ] CI/CD / infra ## Linked Issue/PR - Closes #13373 (per-thread session mode feature request) - Closes #41788 (Google Chat replies creating new threads instead of staying in the existing one) - Related #44347 — resolves the first of the two requests in that issue - [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression ### Note on naming vs the issue's proposal The issue proposes `threadSessionMode: "per-thread" | "per-space"`. This PR ships the same behavior under a boolean flag `sessionThread: boolean` (default `false` = per-space, `true` = per-thread). Rationale: - A boolean matches the two-state nature of the option and is simpler to document. - The name aligns with the existing session-scoping vocabulary in the codebase. - Happy to rename to `threadSessionMode` with a string enum if maintainers prefer the issue's exact wording, it's a straightforward rename. ## Root Cause (if applicable) - Root cause: The Google Chat channel used the space id as the session peer id and did not pass the inbound thread name back on outbound messages. That coupling meant (a) all threads in a space mapped to one session, and (b) replies could fall back to a new thread instead of the user's. - Missing detection / guardrail: No peer-id unit coverage for Google Chat; Slack already has `prepare.thread-session-key.test.ts` as prior art for this exact pattern, but nothing equivalent existed for Google Chat. - Contributing context (if known): Google Chat threads were less prominent historically in OpenClaw flows; the space-scoped default was acceptable until users started relying on threads to separate topics. ## Regression Test Plan (if applicable) - Coverage level that should have caught this: - [x] Unit test - [ ] Seam / integration test - [ ] End-to-end test - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient - Target test or file: `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.session-thread.test.ts` - Scenario the test should lock in: `resolveGoogleChatPeerId` returns the thread name when `sessionThread` is enabled and an inbound thread is present; falls back to `spaceId` otherwise; and produces distinct peer ids for distinct threads so sessions do not cross. - Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: The peer id is the single point where "which session does this message belong to?" is decided for Google Chat. Locking its behavior at the helper boundary catches the regression without pulling in the full monitor stack. - Existing test that already covers this (if any): None for Google Chat. Slack's `prepare.thread-session-key.test.ts` covers the analogous primitive. ## User-visible / Behavior Changes - New opt-in config: `channels.googlechat.sessionThread` (default `false`). - `false` (default): space-scoped sessions, prior behavior unchanged. - `true`: one OpenClaw session per Google Chat thread; a new thread starts a fresh conversation. - Outbound messages now consistently target the inbound thread via `thread.name` + `messageReplyOption=REPLY_MESSAGE_FALLBACK_TO_NEW_THREAD`, so replies land in the user's thread more reliably. This applies regardless of `sessionThread`. ## Diagram (if applicable) ```text sessionThread: false (default, unchanged) space S, thread A -> session(peer=S) space S, thread B -> session(peer=S) # shared memory sessionThread: true space S, thread A -> session(peer=A) space S, thread B -> session(peer=B) # isolated memory space S, no thread -> session(peer=S) # falls back to space-scoped ``` ## Security Impact (required) - New permissions/capabilities? No - Secrets/tokens handling changed? No - New/changed network calls? No (same Chat API endpoints; only request payload now sets `thread.name` and `messageReplyOption`) - Command/tool execution surface changed? No - Data access scope changed? No (in fact, `sessionThread: true` narrows memory scope per thread) ## Repro + Verification ### Environment - OS: macOS - Runtime/container: Node 22 / local gateway (`pnpm openclaw gateway restart`) - Model/provider: any (provider-agnostic) - Integration/channel (if any): Google Chat - Relevant config (redacted): ```jsonc { "channels": { "googlechat": { "enabled": true, "serviceAccountFile": "/path/to/service-account.json", "sessionThread": true } } } ``` ### Steps 1. In a Google Chat space, mention the bot in thread A and ask an identifying question (e.g. "remember the color red"). 2. Start a new thread B in the same space and ask "what color did I mention?". 3. Reply again inside thread A and ask the same question. ### Expected - `sessionThread: true`: in thread B, the bot has no memory of thread A. In thread A, the bot still remembers "red". Replies land in the thread the user messaged in. - `sessionThread: false` (default): behavior is unchanged from prior releases. ### Actual - Matches expected for both modes. ## Evidence - [x] Failing test/log before + passing after ``` pnpm test extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.session-thread.test.ts ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns spaceId when sessionThread is disabled ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns spaceId when sessionThread is undefined (default) ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns thread name when sessionThread is enabled and inbound has a thread ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId falls back to spaceId when sessionThread is enabled but inbound has no thread ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId produces distinct peer ids for distinct threads so sessions don't cross Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 5 passed (5) ``` - [ ] Trace/log snippets - [x] Screenshot/recording - When disabled(previous behavior): - When enabled: - [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant) ## Human Verification (required) - Verified scenarios: - Manually verified in a real Google Chat space against a local gateway: - Bot replies land inside the user's inbound thread (both existing threads and thread-starter messages). - With `sessionThread: true`: new thread = fresh session; prior thread keeps its own context; no cross-thread memory leakage. - With `sessionThread: false`: unchanged, space-scoped memory. - Edge cases checked: - Inbound message with no thread (thread-starter): falls back to space-scoped session as designed. - Two concurrent threads in the same space maintain separate sessions. - What you did **not** verify: - Bot-initiated outbound into a space with no prior inbound thread context (no webhook-origin thread). This PR intentionally does not introduce a `threadKey` fallback for that case; the follow-up work below can add richer binding if demand emerges. - DM flow (no behavior change expected; DM scope is already per-channel-peer). ## Review Conversations - [x] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR. - [x] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment. ## Compatibility / Migration - Backward compatible? Yes - Config/env changes? Yes, additive only: new optional `channels.googlechat.sessionThread` boolean (default `false`). - Migration needed? No. Existing configs continue to behave as before. - If yes, exact upgrade steps: N/A. To opt in, set `channels.googlechat.sessionThread: true`. ## Risks and Mitigations - Risk: Users relying on cross-thread memory in a space would lose that if they set `sessionThread: true` without realizing the implication. - Mitigation: Default is `false`; docs call out the per-thread isolation explicitly; the name `sessionThread` signals the intent. - Risk: `resolveGoogleChatPeerId` is a new exported helper surface from the plugin's `monitor.ts`. - Mitigation: Kept it narrow (one pure function) and it is only consumed inside the extension itself; no public SDK subpath added. ## Future Work (non-blocking) This PR adds the minimal primitive, matching Slack's auto thread-scoped session behavior, just gated behind an opt-in flag for Google Chat. A follow-up could align with the Telegram/Discord `session.threadBindings` model (`/focus`, `/unfocus`, `/session idle`, `/session max-age`) on top of this primitive. That work requires registering slash commands in the Chat API app config and wiring `SLASH_COMMAND` events, which is out of scope here.

target.title: fix(acp): treat missing cwd as stale bound session
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: a bound ACP session can stay attached after its persisted runtime working directory disappears, so retries keep failing against a dead session and the conversation stays wedged.
- Why it matters: affected conversations remain wedged until the stale binding state is manually cleared.
- What changed: during ACP dispatch, treat a generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` as stale when the bound session's persisted `runtimeOptions.cwd` can no longer be resolved on disk (`ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR`), then unbind the dead conversation. The signal is folded into the existing `isStaleSessionInitError` classifier and the existing `maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations` dispatch helper — no new module, no parallel helper.
- Scope: dispatch-only. Two files: `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts` and its test.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- ACP stale-session classifier (`isStaleSessionInitError`) extended to accept the bound session's persisted cwd.
- Auto-reply ACP dispatch stale-binding cleanup (`maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations`) passes the persisted cwd at the `runTurn` catch.
- Regression tests: generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` + missing persisted cwd unbinds; generic init failure + existing cwd does not.

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #60720
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Root Cause

The dispatch path already removes stale ACP bindings for selected ACP session init failures, but it classified staleness from the error message only. The live missing-cwd case surfaces as a generic spawn `ENOENT` wrapped as `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED`, whose message does not match the stale-message set. The reliable signal is the bound session's persisted `runtimeOptions.cwd`: when it no longer resolves to a directory, the binding is unrecoverable. Without checking it, the stale bound conversation survives the failed dispatch and keeps routing future turns into the dead ACP session.

## Implementation Notes

- Rebased onto current `main` after the `@openclaw/acp-core` runtime extraction. The fix now extends `main`'s existing in-file `maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations`/`isStaleSessionInitError` instead of introducing a separate `src/acp/runtime/stale-session.ts` helper (which no longer fits the post-extraction layout). The earlier `extensions/memory-core` test shim is dropped — current `main` carries that mock contract natively.
- Staleness now requires **filesystem-confirmed** absence of the persisted cwd. The unbind cannot be triggered by an error-message string alone, which removes an over-removal vector (e.g. a transient tool error whose text mentions a missing working directory). `ENOENT` and `ENOTDIR` count as missing; a present-but-unreadable cwd (`EACCES`) is treated as present so a transient permission/mount issue never severs a live conversation.

## Maintainer Decision (session-state semantics)

This removes persisted bound-conversation state when a generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` is paired with a filesystem-confirmed missing cwd — the recovery is correct for a permanently gone cwd, but it is session-state behavior worth explicit maintainer acceptance (per ClawSweeper's `merge-risk: session-state`). Two residual, deliberately out-of-scope behaviors to weigh:

- A transient filesystem outage (mount briefly returning `ENOENT`) on a still-valid cwd would unbind a live session. Mitigated by treating only `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` (not `EACCES`) as missing, but not eliminated.

## Summary

- **Problem**: Obsolete `memorySearch` keys (`chunkSize`, `chunkOverlap`, `maxResults`) in `agents.defaults` cause schema validation to fail because the current migration path moves the root key but fails to strip stale sub-keys before `validateConfigObjectWithPlugins` is called.
- **Why it matters**: This blocks gateway startup for users with legacy configs, triggering a ~39k infinite restart loop over 42 hours in production environments.
- **What changed**: Implemented `agents.defaults.memorySearch-obsolete-keys` migration to strip specific stale sub-keys during the runtime migration pass.
- **What did NOT change (scope boundary)**: Internal logic of memory search and per-agent overrides in `agents.list` remain untouched.

- **Root cause**: The `memorySearch` sub-keys were deprecated/removed from the Zod schema, but the migration logic only performed a move operation on the top-level `memorySearch` key. If the keys were already present in `agents.defaults`, they bypassed the move migration and hit the validator as `unrecognized_keys`.
- **Missing detection / guardrail**: Config migration unit tests lacked coverage for partial/obsolete sub-key state within already-migrated root paths.

None (internal config cleanup).

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Before:
[Load] -> [Move Migration (moves root only)] -> [Validation (Fails on sub-keys)] -> [Crash]

After:
```

target.title: Agents/tool-images: memoize resize to avoid per-turn sharp decode (#64418)
target.body:
## Summary

Session history is re-sanitized on every turn via `sanitizeSessionMessagesImages`, which means `resizeImageBase64IfNeeded` is invoked for the same historical image on every message. Both the `getImageMetadata` header read and any `resizeToJpeg` call are expensive sharp decodes, so we memoize the result with a collision-safe, byte-bounded LRU cache.

Fixes #64418.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Skills / tool execution

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #64418
- Related #64514 (prior attempt, auto-closed under `too-many-prs`; this PR addresses both review concerns raised there — see below)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## What's in scope

- Add SHA-256-keyed resize-result cache in `src/agents/tool-images.ts`.
- Eviction by total cached bytes, default 64 MiB, overridable via `OPENCLAW_IMAGE_RESIZE_CACHE_MAX_BYTES`.
- Five new regression tests in `tool-images.test.ts` plus a cache reset in `tool-images.log.test.ts`.

## Addressing #64514 review feedback

#64514 was a prior attempt that was auto-closed under the `too-many-prs` rule, not rejected on merits. Two substantive review concerns were raised there (by `@greptile-apps` and `@chatgpt-codex-connector`); both are addressed upfront here:

- **P1 (cache-key collision).** #64514 hashed only `base64.slice(0, 1000)`, which collides across JPEGs that share SOI + APP0/JFIF + DQT + DHT headers — silently substituting one image's bytes for another's in the model context. This PR hashes the full base64 payload. SHA-256 over several MB is sub-millisecond and still far cheaper than the sharp decode we skip on a cache hit.
- **P2 (unbounded memory).** #64514 used a 200-entry count-based cap, worst-case ≈ 1.3 GB RSS. This PR uses a byte-bounded LRU (64 MiB default), so total cache footprint is fixed regardless of entry size.

Credit to `@EronFan` for the original repro and the call-site integration.

## Tests

- **`keys on the full base64 payload so long shared prefixes do not collide (#64514 P1)`** — direct unit test on `computeResizeCacheKey`. Constructs two strings with a 1024-char identical leading prefix and asserts the keys differ. Mutation-verified: I temporarily patched the keyer to `hash.update(base64.slice(0, 1000))` and confirmed this test fails with `expected '213f2963...' not to be '213f2963...'`, then reverted.
- **`records separate cache entries for two distinct valid images (#64418 end-to-end)`** — wires through `sanitizeContentBlocksImages` with two different valid JPEGs to prove the key is routed through the actual cache wrapper (not just the internal helper).
- **`reuses the resize result for the same image across repeated calls`** — simulates the session-history replay, asserts `misses=1, hits=1` after two calls with the same block.
- **`keys the cache by maxBytes so different limits do not share results`**.
- **`bounds cache memory by evicting past the byte cap`** — deterministic test: sets cap to 1 byte and verifies `entryCount=0, totalBytes <= maxBytes` after three inserts.
- **`tool-images.log.test.ts`** — cache reset added to `beforeEach` so the shared PNG used across tests doesn't let a cache hit silently skip the log lines the tests are asserting on.

## Benchmark

10 turns, same 47 KB PNG (via `tsx`):

| Config | Total | Per turn | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold (cache reset each turn) | 51.9 ms | 5.19 ms | 1× |
| Hot  (cache retained)        | 10.3 ms | 1.03 ms | **5.1×** |

`Image resized to fit limits` log fires **1× instead of 10×** — matches the duplicate-log symptom described in #64418.

## Real Behavior Proof

> **Added 2026-05-18** in response to [ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/68677#issuecomment-4354745918) asking for after-fix evidence beyond the synthetic benchmark above. This section uses the actual `sanitizeContentBlocksImages` function this PR memoizes, with cache stats read back from the same `__testing.getResizeCacheStats()` hook the unit tests use.

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Per #64418, OpenClaw re-decodes the same historical image with sharp on every agent turn because `sanitizeSessionMessagesImages` re-sanitizes the whole session history each turn. Symptom: `Image resized to fit limits` log line fires once per turn instead of once per distinct image. This PR memoizes the resize result keyed by SHA-256 over the full base64 payload (collision-safe) and size limits, with byte-bounded LRU eviction (64 MiB default).

**Real environment tested:** Local node v22.14.0 + sharp built from `pnpm install`. Generated a real 4096x4096 PNG via sharp (228 KB) to make the resize work non-trivial. Imported the actual exports from this PR's `src/agents/tool-images.ts` (`sanitizeContentBlocksImages` + `__testing.{resetResizeCache, getResizeCacheStats}`) — no mocks, no synthetic shortcut.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
1. Rebased onto current `origin/main` (`9817fed842`) → new HEAD `2a177f6e80`. Two real-API rename conflicts resolved (`@mariozechner/*` → `@earendil-works/*`), test helpers merged.
2. `pnpm test src/agents/tool-images.test.ts src/agents/tool-images.log.test.ts` → **17 passed**.
3. Wrote a focused Node driver `src/agents/.proof-image-cache.mts` that: generates a real 4096x4096 PNG with sharp, calls `sanitizeContentBlocksImages([imgBlock], "proof")` 10 times in two scenarios — (a) **cold**: `__testing.resetResizeCache()` between every call (simulates current main where the cache doesn't exist); (b) **hot**: cache retained across calls (this PR's behavior). Times each call with `perf_hooks.performance.now()` and reads back `__testing.getResizeCacheStats()` at the end.
4. `node --import tsx src/agents/.proof-image-cache.mts`.

**Evidence after fix:**

Captured terminal output (redacted of nothing — all values are deterministic synthetic content):

```text
[setup] generating realistic 4096x4096 PNG (cause sharp to do real decode work)…
[setup] generated 233666 bytes (~228 KiB)

[cold] simulating MAIN: reset cache between every turn (same image, decoded N times)
[agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 4096x4096px 228.2KB -> 4.4KB (-98.1%)
[cold turn 1] 195.65 ms
[agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 4096x4096px 228.2KB -> 4.4KB (-98.1%)
[cold turn 2] 89.37 ms
... [8 more identical "Image resized to fit limits" log lines + cold turn timings 70-90 ms each] ...
[cold turn 10] 70.94 ms
[cold] final stats: hits=0 misses=1 entryCount=1

[hot] simulating PR: cache retained across turns (same image, decoded once, cached after)
[agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 4096x4096px 228.2KB -> 4.4KB (-98.1%)
[hot turn 1] 70.82 ms
[hot turn 2] 5.92 ms
[hot turn 3] 6.45 ms
[hot turn 4] 6.47 ms
[hot turn 5] 6.15 ms
[hot turn 6] 6.94 ms
[hot turn 7] 6.23 ms
[hot turn 8] 6.67 ms
[hot turn 9] 6.10 ms
[hot turn 10] 6.30 ms
[hot] final stats: hits=9 misses=1 entryCount=1

============================================================
[summary] 10 turns, single 4096x4096 PNG
[summary] cold total: 876.31 ms (avg 87.63 ms/turn)
[summary] hot  total: 128.03 ms (avg 12.80 ms/turn)
[summary] speedup:    6.84×
[summary] hot cache:  hits=9 misses=1 (expected 9/1)

[PROOF] ✓ resize cache eliminates 9/10 sharp decodes for repeated session-history images
[PROOF] ✓ realized 6.8× speedup on session-history replay of the same image
```

**Observed result after fix:** Three independent signals from real terminal output all confirm the fix:
1. **Cache stats** (read back from `__testing.getResizeCacheStats()`, the same hook the unit tests use): hot scenario shows `hits=9 misses=1` — exactly one decode for 10 invocations of the same image.
2. **Per-turn latency**: cold turns are ~75–90 ms each (real sharp decode), hot turns 2–10 are ~6 ms each (cache hit). Speedup: **6.84×** across 10 turns.
3. **`Image resized to fit limits` log line count**: fires 10× in the cold scenario (the bug symptom), 1× in the hot scenario (the fix). This is the user-visible log-fire-count described in #64418.

**What was not tested:**
- A full openclaw chat session against a live model provider — the driver invokes the same `sanitizeContentBlocksImages` function the agent calls on every turn, but in isolation rather than through the full agent loop. The agent's call path is covered by the existing `sanitizeImageBlocks`/`sanitizeContentBlocksImages` unit tests, plus the cache hit/miss assertions added in this PR's regression suite.
- Behavior under memory pressure beyond the 1-byte eviction unit test — the byte-bounded eviction is unit-tested but not stress-tested with a real-world high-volume image stream.

## Verification

- `pnpm test src/agents/tool-images.test.ts src/agents/tool-images.log.test.ts` — 12 passed (10 + 2)
- `pnpm check` — all gates green (tsgo core + core:test + extensions + extensions:test, oxlint, webhook-body-order, pairing-store-group, pairing-account-scope, import-cycles, madge-import-cycles). Pre-commit hook also ran the full `pnpm check` against the committed tree.
- Linter diagnostics on touched files — 0 errors.
- Rebased onto current `origin/main` (CHANGELOG conflict resolved cleanly — our entry appended after the 5 upstream entries that landed during development).

## Security Impact

No new permissions, secrets/token handling, network calls, command/tool execution surface, or data-access scope changes. The cache holds already-in-memory sanitized image bytes keyed by a SHA-256 hash of those bytes plus the configured size limits; no additional data leaves the process.

## AI-assisted disclosure (per `CONTRIBUTING.md`)

- [x] Built with AI assistance (Cursor + Claude).
- [x] Testing degree: lightly tested (scoped unit + integration tests + mutation test on the collision guard; no repro on a real long session beyond the synthetic benchmark).
- [x] I understand what the code does.

target.title: fix(daemon): avoid loading full gateway logs during diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where gateway diagnostics could load the full stdout/stderr log files just to surface one recent error line. On hosts with large gateway logs, `status`, doctor, or onboarding failure diagnostics could allocate far more memory than needed while still reporting stale errors from the top of an old log.

Related: #79422

## Why This Change Was Made

Gateway diagnostics now read only the last 256 KiB of each resolved log file before scanning for known error patterns or the last non-empty line. This is a read-side bound only: it does not change launchd/systemd logging, log retention, or the error-pattern set from other diagnostics PRs.

## User Impact

Operators still get the most recent actionable gateway diagnostic line, but diagnostic commands no longer need to buffer an entire accumulated gateway log.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` gained an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline and `sanitizeUserFacingText`, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer), no new public SDK surface is added, and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

```
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. new whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
pnpm tsgo:core && pnpm tsgo:core:test: clean
oxlint on changed source files: 0 warnings, 0 errors
oxfmt --check on changed files: all correctly formatted
```

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users viewing Control UI or WebChat sessions could see a failed cron, scheduled, or autonomous agent turn rendered as successful when a later adjacent agent turn produced an assistant reply with no user message between the two turns.

The existing open PR #97873 does not block this narrower replacement: it is currently broad/conflicting and carries unrelated dependency, workflow, release, mobile, docs, and extension changes. This PR rebuilds only the shared chat-item projection fix on current `upstream/main`.

target.title: fix(compaction): count nested toolResult block payloads in estimateTokens
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On tool-heavy sessions, compaction becomes a permanent no-op and the safeguard
hook fires indefinitely (reported in #99375, likely the root cause of #90639).

`countContentBlockChars` in `packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.ts`
only counts blocks of `type: "text"` or `"image"`. Runtimes such as the codex
app-server persist tool results as a nested `type: "toolResult"` content block that
carries its payload in `text`/`content` (see
`extensions/codex/src/app-server/event-projector.ts` → `createToolResultMessage`),
not as a plain `text` block. So `estimateTokens` returns **0** for every tool-result
message, undercounting total context 10–20× on tool-heavy sessions.

Consequence chain from the issue:

1. In `findCutPoint`, backward keep-recent accumulation never reaches
   `keepRecentTokens` (everything estimates ~0), so the cut collapses to the first
   user message in range.
2. `prepareCompaction` then produces an empty `messagesToSummarize`.
3. The compaction-safeguard hook summarizes the whole branch but writes
   `firstKeptEntryId` = the first message, so nothing is ever dropped.
4. The trigger stays true, so compaction re-fires every turn. Only a session reset
   breaks the cycle.

## Why This Change Was Made

Count the nested `toolResult` block's payload in `countContentBlockChars`, so
tool-result messages contribute their real size to the estimate. The codex shape
carries the same string in both `text` and `content`, so the fix prefers `text` and
only falls back to `content` (string or nested array) — the payload is counted once,
never doubled. Text and image blocks are untouched.

## User Impact

Tool-heavy sessions now estimate their true context size, so `findCutPoint` lands a
real cut, compaction actually drops history, and the safeguard stops re-firing every
turn. No change for sessions whose tool results already arrive as plain text/image
blocks.

## Evidence

Regression test `compaction-toolresult-tokens.test.ts` added next to the existing
`compaction-image-tokens.test.ts`: asserts a codex-shaped nested `toolResult` message
estimates `> 0` tokens and equals an equivalent plain-text message (no double count).
Fails before the fix (estimate is 0), passes after.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** `estimateTokens` now counts nested `toolResult` block payloads
instead of returning 0, so tool-result messages contribute their real token estimate.

**Environment tested:** Node v24.18.0 on Windows; production function invoked directly
via `node --import tsx` against the fix branch.

**Steps run after the patch:** Called the actual patched `estimateTokens` from
`packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.ts` on a message built to the
exact codex app-server shape, comparing before/after and against controls.

**Evidence after fix:** Before the patch, the real function returns 0 for a codex-shaped
tool result:

```text
codex toolResult estimateTokens : 0 (undercount -> 0)
```

After the patch:

```text
codex toolResult estimateTokens : 1000 (expect ~1000, was 0 before fix)
canonical text estimateTokens   : 1000 (unchanged control)
image-only toolResult           : 1200 (unchanged control)
```

Regression-test assertions checked against the production function:

```text
tokens>0: true ( 1000 )
equals plain-text (no double count): true ( 1000 vs 1000 )
ASSERTIONS PASS: true
```

**Observed result after the fix:** A 4000-char codex tool result now estimates 1000
tokens (was 0); the payload present in both `text` and `content` is counted once; text
and image controls are unchanged.

**Not tested:** A full live compaction cycle on a running gateway (safeguard firing →
cut point → history drop) was not exercised; verification was against the production
token-estimation function that gates the cut point.

Closes #99375

target.body: ## Summary This PR adds a silent access-request workflow for blocked Telegram and WhatsApp direct messages. - Emit observation-only pre-auth hooks before pairing challenges or rejection. - Support grouped DM allowlists and propagate trusted `sender_group` metadata. - Extend `/allowlist add dm --group` to add senders or move them between groups. - Auto-load trusted bundled or managed `access-request` hooks while keeping mutable workspace hooks explicitly opt-in. - Document a workspace hook example and clean-install troubleshooting requirements. This matters because unknown senders currently have no silent path to request access without entering an agent session or receiving an automatic reply. The intended outcome is a bounded, privacy-conscious pre-auth observation surface that trusted hooks can use for operator-side approval workflows. Out of scope: automatically approving senders, running the model for blocked messages, or auto-enabling mutable workspace hook code. Success means blocked senders remain blocked until manually approved, while a configured phrase can notify the operator without creating a session or reply path. Reviewers should focus on the pre-auth trust boundary, workspace hook opt-in behavior, allowlist normalization, and grouped-entry config handling. ## Linked context Which issue does this close? N/A - no linked issue. Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related? N/A. Was this requested by a maintainer or owner? No known maintainer or owner request. This is an external contribution based on a clean-install access-request workflow. ## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs) - Behavior or issue addressed: Unknown Telegram and WhatsApp DM senders can silently request manual access without creating an agent session, running the model, or receiving a reply. - Real environment tested: Clean Docker Compose OpenClaw installations configured with WhatsApp and Telegram `dmPolicy: "allowlist"` and an explicitly enabled workspace `access-request` hook. - Exact steps or command run after this patch: 1. Configure the workspace `access-request` example with environment variables. 2. Run `openclaw config set tools.profile messaging`. 3. Run `openclaw config set commands.config true`. 4. Recreate the container with `docker compose down && docker compose up -d`. 5. Send the configured access phrase from a blocked WhatsApp number. 6. Approve the sender from the operator chat with `/allowlist add dm --channel whatsapp --group restricted `. - Evidence after fix: 1. WhatsApp blocked sender receives no reply after sending the access phrase. 2. Operator receives the silent WhatsApp access request notification. 3. WhatsApp sender admitted via `/allowlist add dm --channel whatsapp`. 4. WhatsApp admitted sender receives a normal agent response. 5. Telegram blocked sender receives no reply after sending the access phrase. 6. Operator receives the silent Telegram access request notification. 7. target.title: fix: suppress trailing post-message-tool meta-acknowledgements
target.body:
Closes #96681

## What Problem This Solves

After an agent calls the `message` tool (`action=send`) to deliver its main reply, models often append a short trailing meta-acknowledgement -- patterns like `已发 #22141`, `Sent above`, `核心回答如下`, `OK`, `Roger`, `Got it`, and compound forms like `Sent. Replied in thread.`, `已发, 不再追加总结`.

These acks carry no information beyond the message-tool send that already went out, but OpenClaw currently delivers them as a **second** visible message in the channel.

The existing `filterMessagingToolDuplicates` only catches full-content duplicates via substring match with a 10-char minimum, so short meta-acks (e.g. `已发 #22141`, 9 chars) escape the floor and reach the channel as a duplicate message.

## Why This Change Was Made

This patch adds a **complementary** filter -- `filterMessagingToolMetaCommentary` -- that recognizes post-tool-send meta commentary by pattern (Chinese + English) and suppresses it from the final reply payload.

Key design decisions:

1. **Compound ack coverage** -- Two-pass detection: first try full-text anchored patterns, then split on sentence boundaries and verify **every segment** independently matches an ack pattern. Catches `Sent. Replied in thread.`, `已发, 不再追加总结`, `OK. Done.` while **preserving** mixed forms like `OK, that's the fix.`

2. **Only fires after message-tool sends** (`sentTexts.length > 0`). Agents with no message-tool sends are unaffected.

3. **Length-capped at 200 chars** and anchored patterns only -- prefix matches like `Oklahoma weather`, `已发现问题` are not suppressed.

4. **Media payloads always preserved**, even if caption is a meta-ack.

5. **Wired into both paths**: `agent-runner-payloads.ts` (final reply) and `followup-delivery.ts` (queued follow-up).

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (tsx runtime)

```
============================================================
Real Behavior Proof: Post-Message-Tool Meta-Ack Filter
============================================================

[1] Meta-ack pattern detection:
  ✓ "已发 #22141" → true
  ✓ "Sent above" → true
  ✓ "OK" → true
  ✓ "核心回答如下" → true
  ✓ "Sent. Replied in thread." → true
  ✓ "已发, 不再追加总结" → true
  ✓ "OK. Done." → true
  ✓ "Got it. Will do." → true
  ✓ "了解, 收到" → true
  ✓ "OK, that's the fix." → false
  ✓ "Done, the migration is complete." → false
  ✓ "Got it, let me take a look at the code." → false
  ✓ "Oklahoma weather" → false
  ✓ "已发现问题" → false
  Accuracy: 14/14

[2] Pipeline: 3 meta-acks + 1 real reply → filters to 1 payload
  Output: 1 payloads, kept: "Here is the real follow-up analysis..."

[3] Media payloads always preserved:
  1 media payload(s) preserved after filter

✓ All behavior checks passed.
```

### Test coverage (reply-payloads.test.ts)

All **134 tests pass** (includes 109 new test cases for meta-ack detection):

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  134 passed (134)
   Duration  5.10s
```

**Standalone meta-acks covered** (46 positive cases): `已发`, `已发 #22141`, `已发送`, `已发完毕`, `主回复已发`, `消息已发出`, `回复已发`, `好了`, `收到`, `完毕`, `完成`, `了解`, `知道了`, `明白`, `核心回答如下`, `总结如下`, `以下为核心回答`, `以下为总结`, `不再追加总结`, `不再追加`, `以下为回复`, `答案如下`, `如上`, `回复如上`, `Sent`, `Sent above`, `Done.`, `Replied above`, `Replied in thread`, `See above`, `As above`, `Posted.`, `Acknowledged.`, `OK`, `Okay`, `Roger`, `Got it`, `Gotcha`, `Copy that`, `Copied`, `Ack`, `Will do`, `On it`, `Noted`, `Understood`, `Thanks`

**Compound meta-acks covered** (13 cases): `Sent. Replied in thread.`, `已发, 不再追加总结`, `已发. 不再追加.`, `OK. Done.`, `Roger, copy.`, `Done. Sent.`, `收到. 已发.`, `Sent above. Replying in thread.`, `Got it. Will do.`, `已发, 完成`, `OK, noted`, `了解, 收到`, `Copied, thanks`

**False positives excluded** (18+ cases): `Oklahoma weather`, `sentence fixed`, `已发现问题`, `已发现`, `已收到消息`, `sentry deployed`, `okay let's go`, `OK, that's the fix.`, `Got it, let me take a look at the code.`, `Done, the migration is complete.`, `Sent, but I noticed the logs have an error.`, `收到, 但是这个方案有一个问题`, real reply content, and more.

### Build verification

The full project builds successfully with these changes:
```
[build-all] phase timings: total 506.3s
```
No type errors, no build failures.

## Merge Risk

Low. The new filter is additive and only activates when message-tool sends happened this run (`sentTexts.length > 0`). It does not modify the existing dedupe logic. Media payloads are explicitly preserved. The worst-case failure mode is a false positive suppressing a real reply, which the anchored patterns + 200-char limit + compound segment validation guard against.
